tldr: This paper presents a real-world framework for clamping and lifting large objects using bimanual multi-fingered hands from single-view RGB-D images. By generating joint angles for both arms and hands simultaneously via a diffusion model, and pairing this with collision-aware motion planning and force/tactile-guided online refinement, the system achieves stable physical grasps on unseen large objects.
hero_caption: The overall pipeline of the proposed approach. It consists of three phases: multimodal teleoperation data collection (Phase 1), a diffusion model directly predicting arm and hand joint angles from a single-view point cloud (Phase 2), and grasp execution combining collision-aware trajectory planning with force- and tactile-guided online grasp refinement (Phase 3).
overview:
When trying to transport large cardboard boxes, buckets, or balls with a robot, single-arm grippers or hands fall short in both size and payload capacity. Cooperative bimanual grasping—wrapping around the object from both sides using dual arms and multi-fingered hands like humans do—is essential. However, most prior research has focused on tasks with asymmetric roles for each hand, such as pouring or folding. Studies that squeeze and lift a single large object between both hands have mostly remained confined to simulation. In real environments, it is difficult to acquire a complete 3D object mesh from a single camera, and systems struggle with robot reachability constraints as well as contact discrepancies during execution.

To address this, the authors developed an integrated framework capable of bimanual grasping of large objects on physical hardware using only single-view RGB-D camera inputs. First, using Apple Vision Pro teleoperation, they constructed a high-quality real-world grasp dataset containing joint angles, RGB-D images, joint torques, and tactile signals. Based on this, they trained a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) that directly generates a 26-dimensional target joint configuration—7 DoF for each arm and 6 DoF for each hand—straight from partial point clouds. Furthermore, during execution, they introduced waypoint generation to avoid table collisions, along with force-guided refinement that closes the arms until contacting the object and curls each finger according to fingertip tactile and joint torque readings.

In experiments on a physical humanoid upper-body robot, the system achieved high grasp success rates on unseen large objects with diverse geometries and poses not included in training. It significantly outperformed simulation-based baselines and single-hand grasping methods, and ablation studies demonstrated the critical role that motion planning and force-guided contact refinement play in stable real-world grasping.
contributions: Built a DDPM-based grasp generation model that directly predicts all joint angles for both arms and multi-fingered hands (26 DoF in total) from single-view RGB-D partial point clouds.

Constructed and released a real-world large-object grasp dataset consisting of 33 objects across 353 trials, capturing multi-fingered joint angles, vision, torques, and tactile signals via Apple Vision Pro teleoperation.
Achieved high grasp success rates on real hardware by integrating collision-avoiding trajectory planning with online refinement based on inward arm movement and per-finger force/tactile feedback.

sections.heading: Why is grasping large objects with two multi-fingered hands so difficult?
sections.summary: Transporting large everyday objects requires bimanual cooperative grasping, but past robotics research has skewed toward single-arm grasping or simulation environments. This section outlines the challenges of executable, stable bimanual grasping from single-view vision in the real world and introduces the proposed approach.
sections.details:
In robotic manipulation, grasping with parallel grippers or suction cups is widespread, but it hits a wall when targets become complex, large, or unstructured. Multi-fingered dexterous hands offer delicate contact through high degrees of freedom and tactile sensing, but most research on them has focused on relatively small objects graspable with a single hand.

However, trash bins, large balls, and cardboard boxes cannot be grasped with one hand even by humans; they must be clamped and lifted from both sides using two arms. Despite the importance of cooperative bimanual grasping for such large objects, existing efforts have largely stayed in simulation. There are three major real-world barriers:

- Dependence on complete 3D object models: Many existing methods assume complete 3D meshes, but real environments only provide partial point clouds from a single-view camera, accompanied by severe self-occlusions.
- Disregard of robot reachability and feasibility: Generated grasp poses often collide with the table or exceed the arm's workspace limits, making them unexecutable on hardware.
- Lack of execution-time adaptability: Open-loop, feedforward visual control easily fails because even slight pose estimation errors lead to insufficient contact force, causing the object to slip during lifting.

To overcome these hurdles, this paper proposes a real-world framework combining multimodal data collection via teleoperation, target joint configuration generation from single-view point clouds using a diffusion model, and motion planning integrated with online force-guided contact refinement.

sections.heading: At the intersection of dexterous hands and bimanual manipulation: Prior limits and this work's role
sections.summary: This section surveys prior work in dexterous hand grasping and bimanual manipulation. The novelty of this study lies in combining physical hardware, single-view perception, and multi-fingered hands to clamp single large objects, overcoming simulation dependence and simple-gripper limitations.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into two lineages: dexterous hand grasping and bimanual manipulation.

In dexterous hand grasping, the field has shifted from classical analytical methods that solve geometric and physical constraints to data-driven deep learning approaches. Recently, diffusion models have been applied to generate diverse, natural grasp poses. However, most are trained on simulation data for single-hand grasping. For example, BimanGrasp-DDPM tackles bimanual grasping with diffusion models, but it is confined entirely to simulation and relies on full 3D meshes, making direct hardware deployment difficult.

Meanwhile, bimanual manipulation research has largely focused on tasks with asymmetric hand roles, such as pouring or folding cloth. While some works tackle cooperative bimanual grasping using rigid parallel grippers (such as COMBO-Grasp or Bi-Touch), they cannot achieve the compliant wrapping hold that multi-fingered hands provide over wide contact areas.

Among methods that execute real bimanual dexterous grasping of a single large object, reinforcement learning approaches like ViSiL-HD exist; however, they specialize in cuboids, generalize poorly to unseen shapes, and assume hands must slip underneath the object, failing on objects resting flush on a tabletop. This study bridges these gaps by combining real teleoperation data, single-view point cloud conditioning, and force-guided feedback.

sections.heading: A three-stage pipeline: From data collection to grasp generation and force-guided refinement
sections.summary: This section details each phase of the framework: multimodal teleoperation data collection (III-A), a diffusion model generating 26-DoF joint angles from single-view point clouds (III-B), and waypoint trajectory planning combined with force/tactile online refinement (III-C).
sections.details:
The proposed approach consists of three phases: data collection, grasp generation, and grasp execution.

### III-A Dataset Collection
The robotic platform uses the upper body of a Unitree H1-2 humanoid (7 DoF per arm) equipped with Inspire RH56DFTP dexterous hands (6 DoF per hand). Each hand features joint torque sensors at the base of every finger, alongside distributed tactile sensors on the finger pads and palm. An operator wears an Apple Vision Pro headset, teleoperating the robot via real-time retargeting of hand poses and finger joint angles. The sequence of approaching, grasping, lifting, and placing was recorded at 15 Hz to gather multimodal data, including commanded/measured joint angles, head-camera RGB-D images, joint torques, and tactile signals. In total, 353 successful trials were collected across 33 distinct large objects in varied placements and orientations.

### III-B Grasp Generation via Diffusion Model
From a single-view RGB-D frame, the target object region is segmented using the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and foreground pixels are back-projected into 3D space using depth data to form a partial point cloud $\mathcal{P}$. This is passed through a PointNet++ encoder to extract a 1024-dimensional global geometric feature vector $\mathcal{O}$.
The grasp configuration is formulated as a 26-dimensional joint angle vector $\mathbf{h} \in \mathbb{R}^{26}$, combining both arms ($7 \times 2 = 14$ DoF) and both hands ($6 \times 2 = 12$ DoF). Directly predicting joint angles rather than end-effector Cartesian poses avoids the instability and ambiguity of real-robot inverse kinematics (IK) solvers. A Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) is trained in this 26D space to denoise standard Gaussian noise conditioned on the geometric feature $\mathcal{O}$. Finally, predicted joint angles are clipped within the physical range of each actuator.

### III-C Grasp Execution and Force-Guided Refinement
When executing the generated configuration, simply interpolating from the current state to the target joint angles can cause arms to strike the table or fingers to knock the object out of place. To avoid this, a collision-free trajectory is interpolated at 50 Hz through intermediate waypoints: a clearance waypoint $q_1$ that lifts and spreads the arms to avoid table collision, and a pre-grasp waypoint $q_2$ offset along the palm normal from the target pose.
After reaching the target pose, two stages of force-guided refinement take place. First, both arms move slowly inward toward the center point between the two palms until physical contact blocks the motion. Next, readings from the joint torque sensor $J_i$ at the base of each finger (10 fingers total) and the fingertip tactile sensor $T_{i,j}$ are monitored; any finger below its contact threshold is curled incrementally by $\Delta\theta_i$. This loop runs until all fingers register stable contact, producing an adaptive, snug grip that conforms to the object's surface irregularities.

sections.heading: Real humanoid validation: Generalization to unseen objects and the decisive impact of force refinement
sections.summary: In physical experiments on unseen large objects, the proposed framework significantly outperformed simulation-based and single-hand baselines. Ablation studies and force-sensor analyses highlight why motion planning and contact feedback are indispensable.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup and Baselines
The dataset objects were split into 80% for training and 20% for testing, and evaluations were conducted on unseen objects on the real robot. Five different placements and orientations were tested per object, with 3 trials per configuration (15 trials per object) to compute success rates. The success criterion was strict: lift the object at least 5 cm above the table, hold it stably for 2 seconds without slipping or shifting, and complete the action within 30 seconds.
Baselines included BimanGrasp-DDPM (simulation-based bimanual grasp generation), ViSiL-HD (reinforcement learning-based real bimanual grasping), GraspNet (single-gripper grasping), and DexGraspAnything (single dexterous hand grasping).

### IV-B Results and Ablations
The proposed method achieved high success rates across most test objects, whereas baseline methods struggled in the real world:
- BimanGrasp-DDPM failed to generate plausible poses from single-view partial point clouds due to its full-mesh assumption; IK errors and trajectory collisions drastically lowered its success rate.
- ViSiL-HD could not generalize beyond cuboids because it was trained solely on boxes, and its strategy of wedging hands under the object failed on items resting flat on the table.
- Single-arm methods (GraspNet and DexGraspAnything) failed completely on wide boxes and basketballs where single-hand grasp points could not span the object width, confirming the necessity of bimanual grasping (with rare exceptions like thin-rimmed buckets).

Ablation studies demonstrated the necessity of each system component:
- Disabling inward arm squeezing or force-guided finger refinement caused objects to slip and drop due to insufficient contact pressure. Sensor measurements confirmed that while fingertip tactile values were nearly zero before refinement, both joint torques and tactile signals rose sharply across all fingers after refinement, establishing firm contact.
- Omitting motion planning led to frequent failures where arms crashed into the table moving directly from the home pose, or hands pushed the object away during approach.
- Replacing the diffusion model with a heuristic grasp that simply squeezes around the geometric center yielded insufficient grasp force because it could not adapt to local shapes.

Reported failure cases mainly involved extreme object placements near the edge of the robot's workspace, and large heavy boxes (e.g., box 3) grasped far from their center of mass, where the robot could not counterbalance the gravitational torque and the object slipped.

sections.heading: Conclusion and what's next: From static pose generation to dynamic whole-body coordination
sections.summary: The paper demonstrates the success of cooperative bimanual dexterous grasping of large objects in the real world from single-view RGB-D inputs. Future directions include dynamic whole-body trajectory generation and integrating tactile-force signals directly into the learning loop.
sections.details:
This work introduced a real-world bimanual grasping framework that integrates multimodal teleoperation data collection, DDPM-based 26-DoF joint configuration generation conditioned on single-view point clouds, and collision-aware motion planning coupled with force- and tactile-guided online refinement. By bypassing the need for full 3D models and addressing physical robot constraints and contact uncertainty, the system reliably picks up unseen large objects on hardware.

For future work, the authors plan to move beyond static target joint predictions toward end-to-end models that generate entire continuous trajectories throughout the grasp execution. Additionally, while tactile and force feedback are currently handled by rule-based controllers during execution, incorporating them directly into the policy learning process will aim for more physically adaptive manipulation behaviors.

takeaways: Diffusion models can reliably predict 26-DoF joint configurations for dual arms and dexterous hands directly from single-view partial RGB-D point clouds.
Achieving successful hardware execution requires pairing open-loop visual predictions with collision-avoiding waypoint planning and online refinement using contact force and tactile feedback.
Predicting directly in joint angle space rather than end-effector poses (SE(3)) sidesteps the kinematic singularities and discontinuous solutions common to dual-arm dexterous IK.
limitations: The current setup assumes relatively clean tabletop environments with uniform backgrounds and centered objects; cluttered environments will require enhanced segmentation and obstacle avoidance.
The model only generates static final grasp configurations rather than end-to-end dynamic whole-body trajectories from approach through lift.
The system does not estimate object mass or center of mass; grasping heavy objects far from their balance point can lead to slippage caused by gravitational torque.
